name: The Iolani Palace Banyan

location.address: Iolani Palace grounds, 364 S. King St., Honolulu, HI 96813 (mauka/inland side of the grounds)

access: Free. The 11-acre Iolani Palace grounds are open to the public without a ticket (Tue-Sat; check iolanipalace.org for current hours); only the guided tour of the palace interior requires paid admission.
transport: TheBus routes serve downtown Honolulu; Iolani Palace is about a 10-minute walk from the Aloha Tower / Chinatown area.
verify_notes: Register: Hawaii Exceptional Trees list, id 388, species Indian Banyan, locality 'Iolani Palace, 364 S. King St. (Downtown)', girth 2194.6cm, diameter 699.0cm (consistent with each other via circumference=pi*diameter, so this is a real, very large figure), vitality Good. This banyan is multi-trunked (imagesofoldhawaii.com and thelivingurn.com/hawaii-aloha.com both independently describe it as having roughly 16 major trunks fused around a central original trunk), so the register's huge girth is the aggregate circumference of the whole fused cluster, not a single trunk; say so rather than repeating it as one trunk's measurement. Two accounts, both travel/history blogs rather than a primary academic source, agree the tree is 'the most prominent tree on the mauka side of the Palace grounds' and was a gift connected to King Kalakaua's construction of the palace (1879-1882): one credits Queen Kapiolani with planting it, another says it was a gift from Indian royalty to Kalakaua, with Kapiolani again named as the one who planted it. Both dates converge on the Kalakaua building era (early 1880s), giving a broad estimate of roughly 140 years by 2026 (age_min/max 130-150), kept wide because the planter is genuinely disputed even though the era is not. Cuttings from this tree were reportedly planted at Kailua Bay in Kona and at Hulihe'e Palace, per the same sources. No Wikipedia mention of the tree found (checked the Iolani Palace article directly). Alive-now evidence: the palace's own current events page (iolanipalace.org) markets 'Banyan Terrace' as a rentable event space under this exact tree today, so it is a maintained, current landmark rather than a stale record. Access confirmed via Iolani Palace's own site and general search: the 11-acre grounds are free and open Tue-Sat, only the interior palace tour is ticketed; State Parks lists broader grounds hours (6am-6pm). Exact tree-level coordinate not found; pin anchored on the palace's own geocoded address and marked approximate, tree stands somewhere on the mauka (inland/makai-ambiguous, sources say 'mauka') portion of the grounds.

name: The Queen's Medical Center Pink Bombax

location.address: The Queen's Medical Center grounds, near the roundabout, 1301 Punchbowl St., Honolulu, HI 96813

access: Free. Queen's Medical Center's outdoor grounds (a hospital campus) are open to the public; the tree stands outdoors near the roundabout, not inside any building.
transport: TheBus routes serve Punchbowl St; about a 10-minute walk from Iolani Palace / downtown Honolulu.
verify_notes: Register: Hawaii Exceptional Trees list, id 667, species Pseudobombax ellipticum, locality 'Queen's Medical Center, 1301 Punchbowl St.', girth 374.9cm, diameter 119.4cm (internally consistent), vitality Good. Honolulu Magazine's 2021 photo feature on the city's Exceptional Trees names this specific tree ('Pink Bombax, right of the roundabout' at Queen's Medical Center), states it was planted by Dr. William Hillebrand (the same Hillebrand connected to Foster Botanical Garden's own Hillebrand Kapok, hnl_003, a genuine historical figure, Honolulu's 19th-century royal physician and botanist) 'to continue Queen Emma's mission to make the hospital grounds welcoming', and gives the age as 'more than 150 years'; kept as a broad floor (150-170) rather than sharpened, since the magazine gives no more precise figure. The magazine describes 'garish' pink blooms in late March resembling shaving brushes, leaves emerging deep red then maturing green, and swelling green-toned bark when actively growing, all good material for the story. Only one independent write-up found beyond the register itself (fraryguitar.com and edohawaii.com describe a baobab at the same hospital, not this tree), so treat the two-source bar as register-plus-one, per the rules. Hospital grounds count as genuinely open per the access test (a hospital garden, no permission needed to walk through). No tree-level coordinate found; register's own grid rounding (21.31,-157.85) is used directly and the pin is approximate, distinct from the hospital's baobab (hnl_014) which has a separately confirmed GPS fix.

name: The Zoo Gate Banyans

location.address: Outside the main entrance to the Honolulu Zoo, 151 Kapahulu Ave., Honolulu, HI 96815 (in Queen Kapiolani Park, not inside the ticketed zoo)

access: Free. These banyans stand outside the zoo's ticket gate, in the public grounds of Kapiolani Park; no zoo admission is needed to reach or sit under them.
transport: TheBus routes serve Kapahulu Ave / Kalakaua Ave; about a 15-20 minute walk from central Waikiki.
verify_notes: Register: Hawaii Exceptional Trees list carries two banyans here as separate rows, id 401 ('mauka tree', girth 2545.1cm, diameter 83.8cm) and id 402 ('makai tree', girth 1645.9cm, diameter 508.0cm), both at 'Honolulu Zoo, outside entrance', vitality Good for both. Folding them into one entry per the register-twins rule: they flank the same entrance and a visitor experiences them as one landmark, per Historic Hawaii Foundation's description of 'a cluster of towering banyan trees' both inside and outside the zoo entrance, and a travel blog (bomackison.com) independently describes sitting on the benches built around the trunk of the banyan just outside the zoo gate. Register pitfall flagged: id 401's diameter (83.8cm) is wildly inconsistent with its own girth (2545.1cm implies a diameter near 810cm via circumference=pi*d), almost certainly a data entry error in the source register; used id 402's internally-consistent figures (girth 1645.9cm, diameter 508.0cm) as the representative measurement and noted the anomaly rather than repeating the bad number. No age or planting date found for either tree; Hawaii's banyans were introduced 'in the late 1800s' generally per bomackison.com, which is a species-level fact, not a planting date for these two specific trees, so age is left empty rather than bridged. Alive-now: both blog and Tripadvisor/Alamy stock imagery (not used as a source, only as informal confirmation) show a large, healthy standing banyan with a bench ring at this location in recent years. Distinct from the banyan grove already published as hnl_007 (Thomas Square) and from Ala Moana's baobab grove (set aside as not a collectible point, see leads); this is a specific, named pair of flanking landmark trees at one gate, which is a compact, findable point rather than a whole grove.
